rice-white-and-wild-cooked-no-added-fat.title: Rice, white and wild, cooked, no added fat

content.title: About
content.content: Rice is a grain harvested from the Oryza sativa plant. White rice is milled to remove the husk and germ, while wild rice consists of seeds of aquatic grasses related to the water lily family. Cooking without added fat preserves most nutrients and keeps the dish low‑calorie.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: White rice is a staple food for more than half of the world’s population.
Wild rice contains more protein and fiber than regular white rice.
Rice can absorb up to three to four times its weight in water during cooking.
In Japan, rice batter is used to make the savory pancake dish okonomiyaki.
There are over 40,000 rice varieties, each with distinct flavor, aroma, and texture.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Rice provides a steady release of energy thanks to its slowly digestible carbs.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: It contains thiamine, niacin, and vitamin B6, which support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: When boiled without oil, rice contains virtually no fat, making it suitable for calorie‑restricted diets.

items.title: Contains magnesium and phosphorus
items.content: These minerals are important for bone health, muscle function, and nerve signaling.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Fiber, especially in wild rice, helps maintain regular bowel movements.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: White rice can cause rapid spikes in blood sugar, so people with diabetes should monitor portion sizes.

items.title: Arsenic content
items.content: Rice from certain regions may contain trace arsenic; rinsing the grains before cooking reduces this risk.

items.title: Lack of fat
items.content: A fat‑free preparation may limit absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins unless paired with healthy fats.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve rice as a side dish with vegetables, meat, or fish, or incorporate it into salads, soups, and pilafs. For added flavor, cook it in broth, add herbs, or season with spices. Wild rice pairs well with nuts and dried fruit for a hearty salad.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep dry rice in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. Cooked rice should be cooled quickly and stored in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days, or frozen for longer storage.

content.title: About
content.content: Sauce NFS is a flavorful tomato sauce blended with a special spice mix, designed to enhance meat, fish, and vegetable dishes. It is made from ripe tomatoes, onion, garlic, vinegar, and a unique blend of spices, delivering a rich, slightly spicy taste.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Sauce NFS was first launched in 2015 as part of a grill‑focused product line.
The recipe uses only natural vinegar with no added preservatives.
NFS partners with local farms to source pesticide‑free tomatoes.
The sauce holds a Halal certification and is suitable for vegetarians.
Packaging is made from recyclable plastic, reducing environmental impact.

items.title: Rich in lycopene
items.content: Tomatoes in the sauce provide lycopene, a powerful antioxidant that supports heart health.

items.title: Low sugar content
items.content: Unlike many ready‑made sauces, NFS contains minimal added sugar.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The sauce supplies vitamin B6 and niacin, important for metabolism.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Garlic and onion promote gastric juice production, aiding digestion.

items.title: No artificial colors
items.content: All colors come naturally from tomatoes and spices.

items.title: Tomato allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to tomatoes or related plants (eggplant, pepper) may react.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: The sauce contains moderate salt; people with hypertension should monitor portions.

items.title: Spicy flavor
items.content: For children and those with sensitive stomachs, use the sauce sparingly.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Sauce NFS works well for marinating meats, as a barbecue base, in pasta, pizza, and as a dip for vegetable snacks. It can also be added to soups and stews to boost flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the sauce in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep it refrigerated and use within 4‑6 weeks. Discard if the smell or color changes.

soupy-rice-with-chicken-puerto-rican-sty.title: Soupy Rice with Chicken, Puerto Rican Style

content.title: About
content.content: Soupy rice with chicken, Puerto Rican style is a traditional island dish featuring rice cooked in a flavorful chicken broth with pieces of chicken, tomatoes, sweet peppers, garlic, and spices such as adobo and cumin. The result is a hearty, slightly spicy and mildly sweet one‑pot meal.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish originated in rural Puerto Rico as a way to stretch leftover chicken with simple pantry staples.
Rice is traditionally simmered in the chicken broth, giving it a richer taste and texture.
Adobo seasoning—a blend of garlic, oregano, mustard powder, and vinegar—is a key flavor component.
It is often served with fried plantains or avocado to balance the savory heat.
Variations may replace chicken with shrimp or other seafood.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Chicken provides complete, high‑quality protein essential for muscle repair and growth.

items.title: Complex carbohydrates
items.content: Rice supplies steady‑release energy, helping maintain stable blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The dish contains thiamine, niacin, and vitamin B6, which support metabolism and nervous‑system health.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Chicken and rice contribute iron, zinc, and magnesium, important for immunity and muscle function.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Tomatoes and sweet peppers add lycopene and vitamin C, which help combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to chicken, experiencing skin or digestive reactions.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared adobo mixes or store‑bought broth can raise sodium levels, which may be a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Chicken must be cooked to an internal temperature of 75 °C (165 °F) to eliminate salmonella.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the hot rice stew in a deep bowl. Garnish with fresh cilantro, a squeeze of lime, or fried plantains for extra flavor. It works well as a main lunch or dinner and is convenient for outdoor meals.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool leftovers in an airtight container and refrigerate for 3‑4 days. Reheat until boiling before serving. The dish can be frozen for up to 2 months, portioned beforehand.

content.title: About
content.content: Green leaf tea is made from unoxidized leaves of Camellia sinensis. It has a light, fresh flavor with herbal notes and a mild bitterness. The tea is usually brewed with water at 70‑80 °C for 2‑3 minutes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Green tea is one of the most consumed beverages worldwide, especially in China and Japan.
The leaves are not fermented, which preserves more polyphenols than black tea.
Traditional Japanese "matcha" is powdered green tea used in tea ceremonies.
In Japan the "Hanami" festival celebrates cherry blossoms while enjoying green tea.
There are over 300 varieties of green tea, differing by growing region and processing method.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Green tea contains catechins, especially EGCG, which help neutralize free radicals.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Regular consumption may help lower LDL‑cholesterol levels.

items.title: Boosts metabolism
items.content: Caffeine and catechins increase fat oxidation, which can aid weight management.

items.title: Enhances brain function
items.content: The combination of caffeine and L‑theanine improves alertness and concentration.

items.title: May reduce risk of certain diseases
items.content: Studies link green tea intake with lower risk of some cancers and type‑2 diabetes.

items.title: Caffeine sensitivity
items.content: High amounts can cause nervousness, insomnia, or rapid heartbeat.

items.title: Drug interactions
items.content: Green tea may enhance the effects of anticoagulants and some blood‑pressure medications.

items.title: Tannin content
items.content: Tannins can reduce iron absorption from plant foods, so people with anemia should drink tea between meals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Place 1‑2 tsp of leaves in hot (not boiling) water, steep for 2‑3 minutes, then strain. You may add lemon, honey, or ginger to taste. For a cold version, chill the brew and serve over ice.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store green leaf tea in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. Keep it away from moisture and strong odors to preserve flavor and beneficial compounds.
